title: Zephaniah

stories.title: 🏙️ Zephaniah 1
summaryBullets: This is the word of the LORD that came to Zephaniah son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah, the son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah son of Amon king of Judah: (1:1).
“I will completely sweep away everything from the face of the earth,” declares the LORD. (1:2).

“I will sweep away man and beast; I will sweep away the birds of the air, and the fish of the sea, and the idols with their wicked worshipers. I will cut off mankind from the face of the earth,” declares the LORD. (1:3).
“I will stretch out My hand against Judah and against all who dwell in Jerusalem. I will cut off from this place every remnant of Baal, the names of the idolatrous and pagan priests — (1:4).
those who bow on the rooftops to worship the host of heaven, those who bow down and swear by the LORD but also swear by Milcom, (1:5).
and those who turn back from following the LORD, neither seeking the LORD nor inquiring of Him.” (1:6).
Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD, for the Day of the LORD is near. Indeed, the LORD has prepared a sacrifice; He has consecrated His guests. (1:7).
“On the Day of the LORD’s sacrifice I will punish the princes, the sons of the king, and all who are dressed in foreign apparel. (1:8).
On that day I will punish all who leap over the threshold, who fill the house of their master with violence and deceit. (1:9).
On that day,” declares the LORD, “a cry will go up from the Fish Gate, a wail from the Second District, and a loud crashing from the hills. (1:10).
Wail, O dwellers of the Hollow, for all your merchants will be silenced; all who weigh out silver will be cut off. (1:11).
And at that time I will search Jerusalem with lamps and punish the men settled in complacency, who say to themselves, ‘The LORD will do nothing, either good or bad.’ (1:12).
Their wealth will be plundered and their houses laid waste. They will build houses but not inhabit them, and plant vineyards but never drink their wine. (1:13).
The great Day of the LORD is near — near and coming quickly. Listen, the Day of the LORD! Then the cry of the mighty will be bitter. (1:14).
That day will be a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of destruction and desolation, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness, (1:15).
a day of horn blast and battle cry against the fortified cities, and against the high corner towers. (1:16).
I will bring such distress on mankind that they will walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the LORD. Their blood will be poured out like dust and their flesh like dung. (1:17).

Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them on the Day of the LORD’s wrath. The whole earth will be consumed by the fire of His jealousy.” For indeed, He will make a sudden end of all who dwell on the earth. (1:18).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 23:4-12: Josiah’s purge of Baal and astral worship.
Amos 8:4-6: Corrupt merchants crushing the poor.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְכָּם (malkam), Greek (LXX): τῷ βασιλεῖ αὐτῶν, Aramaic: מלכם (malkam)
translationNotes.note: Text can read ‘Milcom’ (Ammonite god) or ‘their king’ (and some traditions relate to Molech). The point is mixed worship, swearing by the LORD and also by another power (1:5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַמַּכְתֵּשׁ (ha-maktesh), Greek (LXX): ἡ κοίλη/ὁ λάκκος, Aramaic: מכתשא
translationNotes.note: Name of Jerusalem’s trading district; also a word for ‘mortar’/‘hollow.’ Traders there are targeted (1:11).

translationNotes.term: Search with lamps / settled on the dregs
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲחַפֵּשׂ… בַּנֵּרוֹת (’aḥappēs… ba-nerot) / עַל שְׁמָרֵיהֶם (’al shemareihem), Greek (LXX): ἐκζητήσω… ἐν λύχνοις / ἐπὶ τῶν τρυγῶν, Aramaic: אבחין בשרגין / על שמוריהון
translationNotes.note: Image of a thorough nighttime search; ‘on the dregs/lees’ is a wine metaphor for hardened complacency (1:12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּנַעַן (Kena‘an), Greek (LXX): ἔμπορος, Aramaic: כנענא
translationNotes.note: In some contexts ‘Canaanite’ also means ‘merchant.’ Zephaniah indicts corrupt trade, not ethnicity (1:11).

stories.keyTakeaway: God will sweep away everything from the face of the earth and stretch out his hand against Judah, cutting off the remnant of Baal, the rooftop worshipers of the host of heaven, and those who swear by both the LORD and Milcom; the great Day of the LORD is near, a day of wrath, distress, darkness, and horn blast, when God searches Jerusalem with lamps to punish the complacent, and neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them.

stories.title: 🌑 Zephaniah 2
summaryBullets: Gather yourselves, gather together, O shameful nation, (2:1).
before the decree takes effect and the day passes like chaff, before the burning anger of the LORD comes upon you, before the Day of the LORD’s anger comes upon you. (2:2).
Seek the LORD, all you humble of the earth who carry out His justice. Seek righteousness; seek humility. Perhaps you will be sheltered on the day of the LORD’s anger. (2:3).
For Gaza will be abandoned, and Ashkelon left in ruins. Ashdod will be driven out at noon, and Ekron will be uprooted. (2:4).
Woe to the dwellers of the seacoast, O nation of the Cherethites! The word of the LORD is against you, O Canaan, land of the Philistines: “I will destroy you, and no one will be left.” (2:5).
So the seacoast will become a land of pastures, with wells for shepherds and folds for sheep. (2:6).

The coast will belong to the remnant of the house of Judah; there they will find pasture. They will lie down in the evening among the houses of Ashkelon, for the LORD their God will attend to them and restore their captives. (2:7).
“I have heard the reproach of Moab and the insults of the Ammonites, who have taunted My people and threatened their borders. (2:8).

Therefore, as surely as I live,” declares the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, “surely Moab will be like Sodom and the Ammonites like Gomorrah— a place of weeds and salt pits, a perpetual wasteland. The remnant of My people will plunder them; the remainder of My nation will dispossess them.” (2:9).
This they shall have in return for their pride, for taunting and mocking the people of the LORD of Hosts. (2:10).
The LORD will be terrifying to them when He starves all the gods of the earth. Then the nations of every shore will bow in worship to Him, each in its own place. (2:11).
“You too, O Cushites, will be slain by My sword.” (2:12).
And He will stretch out His hand against the north and destroy Assyria; He will make Nineveh a desolation, as dry as a desert. (2:13).

Herds will lie down in her midst, creatures of every kind. Both the desert owl and screech owl will roost atop her pillars. Their calls will sound from the window, but desolation will lie on the threshold, for He will expose the beams of cedar. (2:14).

This carefree city that dwells securely, that thinks to herself: “I am it, and there is none besides me,” what a ruin she has become, a resting place for beasts. Everyone who passes by her hisses and shakes his fist. (2:15).
crossRefs: Joel 2:1-11: The day of the LORD imagery (darkness, trumpet).
Isaiah 2:12-21: The LORD humbles human pride.
Proverbs 11:4: Riches do not profit in the day of wrath.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹם יְהוָה (yom YHWH), Greek (LXX): ἡμέρα Κυρίου, Aramaic: יוֹם יי
translationNotes.note: A decisive time when God intervenes in judgment and rescue, not just a ‘bad day.’ Here the stress is on judgment (1:14-18).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תִּסָּתְרוּ (tissatteru, ‘be hidden’), Greek (LXX): κρυβῆτε, Aramaic: תִּתְכְּסוּן
translationNotes.note: Hopeful phrase (2:3). Zephaniah’s name (‘YHWH hides’) echoes this theme of protection for the humble.

Two small kingdoms east of the Dead Sea and the lower Jordan, descended from Lot's two daughters and named for his grandsons in Genesis 19:36-38. They were blood relations of Israel and hostile for most of their history. Each had a national god, and Solomon built a high place for both on the hill east of Jerusalem: Chemosh for Moab and Milcom, also called Molech, for Ammon (1 Kings 11:5-7). Numbers 21:29 calls the Moabites the people of Chemosh.

A people of the southern coastal strip, named here alongside the Philistines. 1 Samuel 30:14 puts the Negev of the Cherethites right next to the territory of Judah. David recruited from them: the Cherethites and Pelethites under Benaiah son of Jehoiada were his standing bodyguard, and they marched out with him when Absalom seized Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:18; 15:18).

The capital of Assyria, on the east bank of the Tigris. Jonah 3:3 calls it a great city needing a three-day journey to cross, and 2 Kings 19:36 has Sennacherib returning there and staying after his campaign against Jerusalem. Nahum's entire book is a burden against it (Nahum 1:1). Zephaniah 2:13-15 says the city will be left dry as a desert, with owls calling from the windows of what is left.

stories.keyTakeaway: Before the burning Day of the LORD’s anger arrives, the shameful nation is told to gather and the humble to seek the LORD, righteousness, and humility, that they may be sheltered; judgment then falls nation by nation: Philistia’s coast becomes pasture for the remnant of Judah, Moab and Ammon become like Sodom and Gomorrah for taunting God’s people, Cush falls by the sword, and carefree Nineveh is left a desolation where herds lie down.

stories.title: 🎶 Zephaniah 3
summaryBullets: Woe to the city of oppressors, rebellious and defiled! (3:1).
She heeded no voice; she accepted no correction. She does not trust in the LORD; she has not drawn near to her God. (3:2).
Her princes are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves, leaving nothing for the morning. (3:3).
Her prophets are reckless, faithless men. Her priests profane the sanctuary; they do violence to the law. (3:4).
The LORD within her is righteous; He does no wrong. He applies His justice morning by morning; He does not fail at dawn, yet the unjust know no shame. (3:5).
“I have cut off the nations; their corner towers are destroyed. I have made their streets deserted with no one to pass through. Their cities are laid waste, with no man, no inhabitant. (3:6).
I said, ‘Surely you will fear Me and accept correction.’ Then her dwelling place would not be cut off despite all for which I punished her. But they rose early to corrupt all their deeds. (3:7).

Therefore wait for Me,” declares the LORD, “until the day I rise to testify. For My decision is to gather nations, to assemble kingdoms, to pour out upon them My indignation — all My burning anger. For all the earth will be consumed by the fire of My jealousy. (3:8).
For then I will restore pure lips to the peoples, that all may call upon the name of the LORD and serve Him shoulder to shoulder. (3:9).
From beyond the rivers of Cush My worshipers, My scattered people, will bring Me an offering. (3:10).

On that day you will not be put to shame for any of the deeds by which you have transgressed against Me. For then I will remove from among you those who rejoice in their pride, and you will never again be haughty on My holy mountain. (3:11).
But I will leave within you a meek and humble people, and they will trust in the name of the LORD. (3:12).
The remnant of Israel will no longer do wrong or speak lies, nor will a deceitful tongue be found in their mouths. But they will feed and lie down, with no one to make them tremble.” (3:13).
Sing for joy, O Daughter of Zion; shout aloud, O Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart, O Daughter of Jerusalem! (3:14).
The LORD has taken away your punishment; He has turned back your enemy. Israel’s King, the LORD, is among you; no longer will you fear any harm. (3:15).
On that day they will say to Jerusalem: “Do not fear, O Zion; do not let your hands fall limp. (3:16).
The LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save. He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing.” (3:17).
“I will gather those among you who grieve over the appointed feasts, so that you will no longer suffer reproach. (3:18).
Behold, at that time, I will deal with all who afflict you. I will save the lame and gather the scattered; and I will appoint praise and fame for the disgraced throughout the earth. (3:19).

At that time I will bring you in; yes, at that time I will gather you. For I will give you fame and praise among all the peoples of the earth when I restore your captives before your very eyes,” says the LORD. (3:20).
crossRefs: Isaiah 35:3-10: The ransomed return; the lame healed.
Zephaniah 2:3: The humble seeking the LORD.
Acts 2:5-11: Many languages confessing the LORD (worship across tongues).
Revelation 21:3-4: God with His people; tears removed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׂפָה בְרוּרָה (safah berurah), Greek (LXX): χεῖλος καθαρόν, Aramaic: ספא דנקיא
translationNotes.note: Cleansed speech for united worship; not a claim that all languages are erased (3:9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵעֵבֶר לְנַהֲרֵי כּוּשׁ, Greek (LXX): ἐπέκεινα ποταμῶν Αἰθιοπίας, Aramaic: מעבר נהרי כוש
translationNotes.note: Distant south lands (Nubia/Ethiopia region). God draws worshipers from far away (3:10).

translationNotes.term: He will quiet/renew you in His love
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יַחֲרִישׁ בְּאַהֲבָתוֹ, Greek (LXX): ἀνακαιιεῖ ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ, Aramaic: ישקיט במחבבתיה
translationNotes.note: Hebrew can mean ‘quiet’ (soothe) or, in textual tradition reflected in LXX, ‘renew.’ Both express tender, restoring care (3:17).

translationNotes.term: The King of Israel, the LORD, in your midst
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה בְּקִרְבֵּךְ, Greek (LXX): βασιλεὺς Ἰσραήλ Κύριος ἐν μέσῳ σου, Aramaic: מלכא דישראל יוי בגוויך
translationNotes.note: Divine-royal title: God Himself is present as Israel’s King (3:15).

stories.keyTakeaway: After judgment, God purifies speech, gathers scattered worshipers, leaves a humble remnant, and personally rejoices over Zion. He removes shame and restores His people.

intro:
Zephaniah was written by Zephaniah son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah (Zephaniah 1:1), during the early reign of King Josiah of Judah (640-609 BC). The book was composed before Josiah's major religious reforms of 622 BC, which were triggered by the discovery of the Book of the Law in the temple (2 Kings 22-23; 2 Chronicles 34); Zephaniah's denunciations of idolatry and syncretism in Jerusalem assume the corrupt religious conditions that prevailed before those reforms. This places the composition between roughly 640 BC and 625 BC. The unusual four-generation genealogy in Zephaniah 1:1, the longest of any canonical prophet's, is best explained by Zephaniah's need to establish his royal Davidic descent: the Hezekiah named four generations back is traditionally identified with King Hezekiah of Judah (715-686 BC), making Zephaniah a great-great-grandson of that king and a member of the extended royal family. His Hebrew name Tzfanyah (צְפַנְיָה) means "Yahuah has hidden" or "Yahuah has treasured up," combining the verb tzafan ("to hide" or "to treasure") with the divine name Yah; some commentators have suggested the name commemorates how the royal line had been hidden or preserved through the bloody purges of King Manasseh (the same Manasseh who, according to 2 Kings 21:16, "shed very much innocent blood, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another"). Zephaniah was a contemporary of the young Jeremiah (whose ministry began in 627 BC, the thirteenth year of Josiah, Jeremiah 1:2) and probably also of Nahum (during the reign of Josiah's grandfather Manasseh). Several other Zephaniahs appear in the Old Testament, none identical with this prophet: Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, a priest in Jerusalem during Jeremiah's time who was taken to Riblah and executed by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC (Jeremiah 21:1; 52:24-27); Zephaniah the Kohathite Levite (1 Chronicles 6:36-38), an ancestor of the prophet Samuel; and Zephaniah father of Josiah, a post-exilic figure in Jerusalem (Zechariah 6:10, 14).

The historical setting is the tail end of the Neo-Assyrian Empire and the period of Josiah's reforms in Judah. The two kings preceding Josiah had been disasters for Judahite worship: Manasseh of Judah (697-642 BC) reversed his father Hezekiah's reforms, restored the Baal and Asherah cults, set up idolatrous altars in the very temple of YHWH, practiced child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, and consulted mediums (2 Kings 21:1-9; 2 Chronicles 33:1-9); 2 Chronicles 33:11-13 records that he was taken in chains to Babylon by the Assyrians (during the reign of Ashurbanipal, when Babylon was an Assyrian-held city), where he repented and was eventually restored to his throne. Manasseh's son Amon (642-640 BC) returned to idolatry and was assassinated by his own servants after only two years; the people of the land killed the conspirators and placed Amon's eight-year-old son Josiah on the throne (2 Kings 21:19-26). Josiah's reign of thirty-one years (640-609 BC) brought the most thorough religious reform in Judah's history: in his eighth year (632 BC) he began seeking the God of David, in his twelfth year (628 BC) he began purging Judah and Jerusalem of idolatry, and in his eighteenth year (622 BC) the high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law in the temple during renovations, triggering the most intense phase of the reforms (2 Chronicles 34:3-7). Zephaniah's ministry fits the period after Josiah came to the throne but before these reforms had taken full effect. The Assyrian Empire was in its final decline: Ashurbanipal had died around 631 BC, and the Babylonians under Nabopolassar would declare independence in 626 BC, beginning the war that would destroy Nineveh in 612 BC.

Zephaniah is the thirty-sixth book of the Christian Old Testament and the ninth of the twelve Minor Prophets. The Hebrew name Tzfanyah (צְפַנְיָה) is the prophet's own name. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Zephaniah were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), preserved as part of the Twelve Minor Prophets scrolls; the earliest copies date to the 2nd century BC. The medieval Latin hymn Dies Irae ("Day of Wrath," used in the Catholic Requiem Mass) opens with imagery drawn from Zephaniah 1:15 ("That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish"), one of the most influential prophetic passages on Western liturgical poetry.
